title: How does model binding and validation work in ASP.NET Core?
description: Where request data becomes action parameters, how validation runs, and how to extend both.

data.text: **Question:** How does model binding and validation work in ASP.NET Core?

Model **binding** maps incoming data (route, query, form, headers, body) onto action parameters in a defined source order, using type converters and `IModelBinder`s. Model **validation** runs after binding: `ValidationVisitor` checks each bound object against its metadata — DataAnnotations attributes, `IValidatableObject`, and registered `ValidationAttribute`s — accumulating errors into `ModelState`. If anything failed, `ApiController`-attributed controllers automatically return **400 ProblemDetails** before your action executes.

**Binding sources:**
- Default order for simple types: route → query → form body; complex types bind from the body if `[FromBody]`, otherwise form/query
- Attributes pin the source: `[FromRoute]`, `[FromQuery]`, `[FromForm]`, `[FromBody]`, `[FromHeader]`
- Only **one** body source per action; form and body together are invalid
- Custom binders (`IModelBinderProvider`, `TryParse`, `BindAsync`) handle enums-as-strings, `CancellationToken`, or custom value types
- [ApiController] inference: complex → FromBody, primitives → FromQuery, unless overridden

**Validation:**
- Attributes on the model: `[Required]`, `[Range]`, `[StringLength]`, `[RegularExpression]`, `[EmailAddress]`
- Cross-property rules: implement `IValidatableObject.Validate()` or a custom `ValidationAttribute`
- Client-side validation mirrors DataAnnotations when the tag helpers + unobtrusive scripts are included — server validation remains the authority
- For rule sets that don't fit attributes (uniqueness against a database), use a validator library (FluentValidation) wired as `IValidator<T>` and inject it in the action — don't lie to the framework with fake attributes
- Reading `ModelState.IsValid` is unnecessary in `[ApiController]` actions — automatic 400 happens first

**Gotchas:**
- Value types are non-nullable: missing `int Page` binds to 0 — use `int?` or required validation to detect absence
- Validation runs on the **bound** object; fields the binder didn't set keep their defaults
- Collection binding: `?tags=a&tags=b` → string array; JSON body → model deserialization (System.Text.Json options matter: case sensitivity, dates, enums)
- Never trust client-side validation alone; never put secrets in route/query (logged)

data.title: Bound sources and layered validation

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Knowing the binding source order and the role of the [From*] attributes
- Understanding where automatic 400s come from ([ApiController] + ModelState)
- Difference between annotation validation and business-rule validation
- Awareness of value-type/nullability and JSON deserialization pitfalls

items: Checking ModelState.IsValid in [ApiController] actions — the framework already rejected invalid bodies
Relying on client-side validation as a security control
Non-nullable value types silently defaulting when the parameter is missing
Database-dependent rules (uniqueness) crammed into custom ValidationAttributes
Binding the body twice or mixing [FromForm] with [FromBody]
Trusting route/query values that were never validated against allowed formats
How would you validate a rule that needs a database lookup?
What happens when a JSON property name casing doesn't match the DTO?
How do you bind a custom value type like Money or a DateRange?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Binding maps route/query/form/header/body onto parameters; [From*] pins the source
ValidationVisitor applies DataAnnotations/IValidatableObject to bound models
[ApiController] turns invalid ModelState into 400 ProblemDetails automatically
Client-side mirroring is UX; server validation is the contract
data.takeaway: Binding answers 'where did this value come from' and validation answers 'is it acceptable' — keep framework validation for shape and services for business rules.
